questions.stem: An estimate of $500k is priced in 2025 dollars. The work is done and paid for in 2028, and prices for this work rise 4% a year. How much is paid?

options.text: $500.0k, since escalation counts from 2028, the year the work starts
options.says: Counting from the start is the shortcut the page warns about; the exponent counts from the price base year.

options.text: $540.8k, since escalation counts from 2026, the year after the estimate
options.says: The exponent is y - b = 2028 - 2025 = 3; an amount paid in the price base year itself is not escalated, so no year is skipped.

options.text: $562.4k, since escalation counts the three years from 2025 to 2028
$584.9k, since escalation counts the four years from 2025 through 2028
options.says: That counts the base year as a year of rise; the exponent is the difference of the years, 3.

origin.section: Escalation Turns a Price Quoted in One Year Into the Price Paid in Another

questions.stem: A team escalates every cost at general inflation and then discounts the escalated costs at a real rate. Compared with a consistent valuation, what is the present value of the costs?

options.text: Too large, since inflation is put into the flows and never taken out
options.says: Right: nominal flows at a real rate; the page's P022 case is $143k too large.

options.text: Too small, since inflation is taken out by the rate and never put in
options.says: That describes the other mix, real flows at a nominal rate; here the flows are escalated.

options.text: Unchanged, since the escalation and the real rate cancel year by year
options.says: They cancel only for nominal flows at a nominal rate (or real at real); the page's mixed line differs by $143k.

options.text: Too small, since the real rate is lower and so discounts the costs more
options.says: A lower rate discounts less, not more; the page's nominal-flows, real-rate line is the largest of the five.

origin.section: Real Dollars Pair With a Real Rate, Nominal Dollars With a Nominal Rate

questions.stem: A model works in constant base-year dollars. Steel prices are forecast to rise 5% a year while general inflation is 3% a year. At what yearly rate should the model escalate its steel costs?

options.text: 5% a year, since that is the rise the buyers will see on each order
options.says: 5% includes inflation, which a constant-dollar model has already taken out; using it counts inflation twice.

options.text: 0% a year, since a constant-dollar model keeps each cost at base prices
options.says: Only a cost rising exactly with inflation stays flat in constant dollars; steel rises faster.

options.text: About 8.15% a year, since the steel rise is added on top of inflation
options.says: Adding inflation goes the wrong way; the real escalation removes it: (1.05/1.03) - 1.

options.text: About 1.94% a year, since only the rise above inflation is real
options.says: Right: (1 + 0.05)/(1 + 0.03) - 1 = 1.94%, the page's real escalation formula.

origin.section: Only Escalation Above Inflation Changes a Real Model
